sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A circuit breaker is a resilience pattern that wraps a call to a remote service and stops sending traffic when that service is failing — tripping from CLOSED through OPEN to HALF_OPEN — so that a single downstream failure cannot cascade into a system-wide outage, with fallbacks providing graceful degradation.

In a microservices system, every synchronous call is a dependency that can fail or slow down. Without protection, a single slow service causes thread pools to fill, request queues to back up, and the calling service to fail in turn — a cascading failure where one service's outage takes down the whole system. Netflix hit this in 2011–2012: a slow metadata service caused their recommendation service's threads to block, which caused the API gateway's threads to block, which took down the entire site for hours, even though the metadata service itself recovered quickly. The post-mortem led to Hystrix, the first widely-adopted circuit breaker library, which wrapped every remote call and tripped open when the call's error rate exceeded a threshold — once open, calls fail fast (in microseconds) instead of blocking (for seconds), the downstream gets a chance to recover, and the calling service stays responsive. The circuit breaker is now a standard pattern: Resilience4j (the modern Java successor to Hystrix), Envoy's outlier detection, Istio's circuit breakers, and Polly (.NET) all implement it.

The state machine has three states. **CLOSED** is the normal state: calls flow through, and the breaker counts successes and failures in a rolling window (e.g., last 100 calls or last 10 seconds). When the failure rate exceeds a threshold (typically 50% over a sample of 20+ calls), the breaker trips to **OPEN**. In OPEN, all calls are rejected immediately — no network call is made, and the caller gets an exception or a fallback within microseconds. This gives the downstream time to recover (typically 5–60 seconds) without the calling service continuing to pile on requests. After the configured timeout, the breaker transitions to **HALF_OPEN**, where a small number of probe calls (often just one) are allowed through. If the probes succeed, the breaker returns to CLOSED and normal traffic resumes; if they fail, it goes back to OPEN for another timeout period. The state machine is a feedback loop: the breaker learns from recent failures, protects the downstream when it is unhealthy, and tests the water periodically to see if recovery has happened.

The fallback is the second half of the pattern. A circuit breaker without a fallback just converts a slow failure into a fast failure — useful for protecting the calling service's threads, but the user still sees an error. A fallback provides a degraded-but-functional response when the breaker is open: a cached value, a default, a stale-but-acceptable result, or an alternative path. Netflix's recommendation service, when its metadata dependency's breaker is open, falls back to a "popular now" list cached at the edge — the user still sees recommendations, just not personalized ones. A billing service whose fraud-check dependency is open might fall back to a synchronous check that approves transactions below $100 (low risk) and queues larger ones for later review. The fallback must be chosen carefully: it should be cheaper than the original call (so it does not itself become a bottleneck), it should be available (do not fall back to another dependency that is also likely down), and it should be honest about degradation (the user should know they are seeing cached data, not fresh). The architect's rule is that every circuit breaker should have a fallback unless the calling service genuinely cannot continue without the downstream — in which case the breaker is still useful for failing fast, but the user-facing request will fail.

The configuration knobs are the heart of the pattern's effectiveness. **Failure threshold**: the error rate (or absolute count) that trips the breaker — too low and you trip on transient blips, too high and you do not protect in time; 50% over 20 calls is the Hystrix default. **Open duration**: how long the breaker stays open before probing — too short and you hammer a still-failing downstream, too long and recovery is delayed; 5–30 seconds is typical. **Half-open probe count**: how many calls are allowed through in HALF_OPEN — one is conservative, ten is aggressive; the right value depends on the downstream's recovery profile. **Rolling window**: how many recent calls are counted — too short and the breaker is jittery, too long and it is slow to react; 100 calls or 10 seconds is standard. **Which errors count**: only 5xx responses, or also timeouts, or also slow successes (latency above a threshold)? Most breakers count timeouts and 5xx but not 4xx (which are client errors, not downstream failures). The mistake to avoid is configuring the breaker so tightly that it trips on normal variance — a service with 5% error rate under normal load should not trip a 50% threshold, but if the threshold is set to 5%, the breaker will be permanently half-open. The deeper lesson is that the breaker is a circuitous feedback loop: it must be tuned to the downstream's actual failure profile, which means measuring the downstream's normal error rate and latency before configuring the breaker.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CLOSED
    CLOSED --> OPEN: failure_rate > 50%\n(last 20 calls)
    OPEN --> HALF_OPEN: after 10s timeout
    HALF_OPEN --> CLOSED: probe call succeeds
    HALF_OPEN --> OPEN: probe call fails
    CLOSED --> CLOSED: calls pass through
    OPEN --> OPEN: calls fail fast (fallback)
    HALF_OPEN --> HALF_OPEN: probe in flight
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
                       state machine

     +---------+   failure_rate > 50%   +---------+
     | CLOSED  | ----------------------> |  OPEN   |
     | (calls  |                         | (calls  |
     |  flow)  | <---------------------- |  fail   |
     +---------+    probe succeeds       |  fast)  |
         ^          +------ after 10s ---+---------+
         |          |   timeout              |
         |          v                        | probe fails
         |    +-----------+                  |
         +--- | HALF_OPEN | <----------------+
              | (1 probe   |
              |  allowed)  |
              +-----------+

   time-of-failure behavior:

   t=0   downstream starts failing
   t=2s  breaker has 12/20 failures -> trip to OPEN
   t=2s  caller gets fallback (microseconds, not 2s timeout)
   t=12s OPEN timer expires -> HALF_OPEN, probe sent
   t=12s probe fails -> back to OPEN for another 10s
   t=22s probe succeeds -> CLOSED, normal traffic resumes
```

### Walkthrough
1. In CLOSED, calls flow through to the downstream and the breaker tracks success/failure in a rolling window of the last 20 calls; under normal operation the failure rate stays well below the 50% threshold.
2. When the downstream starts failing (timeouts, 5xxs), the failure rate crosses 50% and the breaker trips to OPEN — all subsequent calls fail fast (microseconds) with a fallback, instead of waiting seconds for a timeout.
3. After the open timeout (e.g., 10 seconds), the breaker transitions to HALF_OPEN and allows one probe call; if the probe succeeds, the breaker returns to CLOSED and normal traffic resumes, but if it fails, the breaker goes back to OPEN for another timeout, repeating until the downstream recovers.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Circuit breaker state machine with failure counting, timeout, and fallback.
# Demonstrates CLOSED -> OPEN -> HALF_OPEN -> CLOSED transitions.

import time, random, threading
from collections import deque
from enum import Enum

class State(Enum):
    CLOSED = "CLOSED"
    OPEN = "OPEN"
    HALF_OPEN = "HALF_OPEN"

class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=0.5, window_size=20,
                 open_timeout=10.0, half_open_max_calls=1):
        self.failure_threshold = failure_threshold
        self.window_size = window_size
        self.open_timeout = open_timeout
        self.half_open_max_calls = half_open_max_calls
        self.state = State.CLOSED
        self.recent = deque(maxlen=window_size)   # True=success, False=failure
        self.opened_at = 0.0
        self.half_open_calls = 0
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def _record_success(self):
        with self.lock:
            self.recent.append(True)
            if self.state == State.HALF_OPEN:
                self.state = State.CLOSED
                self.recent.clear()
                print("  [breaker] HALF_OPEN -> CLOSED (probe succeeded)")

    def _record_failure(self):
        with self.lock:
            self.recent.append(False)
            if self.state == State.HALF_OPEN:
                self.state = State.OPEN
                self.opened_at = time.time()
                print("  [breaker] HALF_OPEN -> OPEN (probe failed)")
            elif self.state == State.CLOSED and len(self.recent) >= 5:
                failures = sum(1 for x in self.recent if not x)
                rate = failures / len(self.recent)
                if rate >= self.failure_threshold:
                    self.state = State.OPEN
                    self.opened_at = time.time()
                    print(f"  [breaker] CLOSED -> OPEN (failure rate {rate:.0%})")

    def allow(self):
        with self.lock:
            if self.state == State.CLOSED:
                return True
            if self.state == State.OPEN:
                if time.time() - self.opened_at >= self.open_timeout:
                    self.state = State.HALF_OPEN
                    self.half_open_calls = 0
                    print("  [breaker] OPEN -> HALF_OPEN (timeout elapsed)")
                else:
                    return False
            if self.state == State.HALF_OPEN:
                if self.half_open_calls < self.half_open_max_calls:
                    self.half_open_calls += 1
                    return True
                return False
            return self.state == State.CLOSED

    def call(self, fn, fallback=None, *args, **kwargs):
        if not self.allow():
            print("  [breaker] call rejected (OPEN) -> fallback")
            return fallback() if fallback else None
        try:
            result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
            self._record_success()
            return result
        except Exception as e:
            self._record_failure()
            print(f"  [breaker] call failed: {e}")
            return fallback() if fallback else None

# --- Simulate a flaky downstream that fails 80% of the time for a while ---
def flaky_downstream():
    if random.random() < 0.8:
        raise TimeoutError("downstream timeout")
    return "ok"

def fallback():
    return "cached-default"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cb = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=0.5, window_size=20, open_timeout=2.0)
    for i in range(25):
        result = cb.call(flaky_downstream, fallback=fallback)
        print(f"req {i+1}: {result}")
        time.sleep(0.3)
```

quiz.question: What problem does a circuit breaker solve that retries alone do not?
options: Without protection, the failure cascades in three stages.
The diagnosis is that the downstream can handle a single probe but cannot handle full traffic — it is recovered at low load but fails under load.
Envoy's outlier detection operates per-instance, not per-dependency.

quiz.explanation: Retries handle transient failures (a single dropped packet, a brief GC pause) by re-sending the request, but they make sustained failures worse: if a downstream is overloaded, every retry adds more load, accelerating its failure — the "retry storm" that took down AWS DynamoDB in 2015 and several Stripe outages.

When the failure rate crosses the threshold (e.g., 50% of last 20 calls), the breaker trips to OPEN, where all calls fail fast without hitting the downstream — this protects the downstream from further load and the caller from blocking on slow calls.

Hystrix is a library circuit breaker: the breaker logic runs in the calling service's process, as part of the application code or framework.
quiz.explanation: Hystrix is a library circuit breaker: the breaker logic runs in the calling service's process, as part of the application code or framework. Every language must implement its own (Hystrix for Java, Polly for .NET, opossum for Node, cbreaker for Go), and the breaker's state is per-process — each instance of the calling service has its own breaker state, so if you have 100 instances, each tracks failures independently.

quiz.question: What is a retry storm, and how do circuit breakers and jitter prevent it?
options: Without protection, the failure cascades in three stages.
Envoy's outlier detection operates per-instance, not per-dependency.
The diagnosis is that the downstream can handle a single probe but cannot handle full traffic — it is recovered at low load but fails under load.
A retry storm is a positive-feedback loop where retries amplify load on a struggling downstream, accelerating its failure.
quiz.explanation: A retry storm is a positive-feedback loop where retries amplify load on a struggling downstream, accelerating its failure. The mechanism: a downstream becomes slow, callers time out, callers retry, the downstream now has 2x or 3x the original load (because every original request is duplicated by retries), the downstream gets slower, more callers time out, more retries, the downstream collapses.
